title: Compiling ahead of time
cards/0/body:
On every launch the program spends time turning CIL into machine code. Usually you don't notice, but for large apps and cloud services that restart often, startup time matters.

The fix is to compile in advance: AOT (ahead-of-time).
cards/1/title: NGen: the approach from the Microsoft article
cards/1/body:
Classic .NET Framework had NGen.exe for this. It differs from the JIT in three ways:

1. It compiles before launch, not during.
2. It compiles the whole assembly at once, not one method at a time.
3. It saves the code to disk, in the Native Image Cache, and different processes can share it.
cards/2/pairs/0/1: Compiles a method on its first call
cards/2/pairs/1/1: Compiles the whole assembly in advance
cards/2/pairs/3/1: Hands the first call to the JIT
cards/3/body:
NGen exists only in .NET Framework. .NET 5 and later offer two options:

ReadyToRun: the file contains precompiled machine code plus CIL, just in case. Startup is faster, and the JIT can later reoptimize hot methods. Property: <PublishReadyToRun>.

Native AOT: the whole program becomes a single native file. There is no JIT in it at all, and you don't need .NET installed. Property: <PublishAot>.
cards/3/deep: Native AOT requires trimming: the compiler throws away everything it can't reach statically. Hence the limits: no Assembly.LoadFrom or Reflection.Emit, and reflection over types never mentioned in code may fail to find them. Analyzers flag the risky spots with IL2xxx and IL3xxx warnings.
cards/4/task: Press "Start" and see who prints 42 first.
cards/5/q: Why is a ReadyToRun file bigger than a regular one?
cards/5/options/0: It holds both precompiled machine code and CIL
cards/5/options/1: All of .NET is built into it
cards/5/explain: The CIL is kept so the JIT can recompile code if the precompiled version doesn't fit or the method gets hot.
cards/5/wrong/1: Native AOT carries the whole runtime inside. ReadyToRun still relies on the installed .NET.
cards/6/q: An app loads plugins from a folder at run time (Assembly.LoadFrom) and generates code (Reflection.Emit). Will Native AOT work?
cards/6/options/0: No: Native AOT can't load or create code at run time
cards/6/options/2: Yes, if you turn on ReadyToRun
cards/6/explain: Native AOT has no JIT, so there is nothing to compile new code at run time.
cards/7/q: You want faster startup but don't want to change your code. What do you turn on?
cards/7/explain: ReadyToRun is compatible with everything: if the precompiled code isn't enough, the regular JIT steps in.
cards/7/wrong/1: Native AOT may need code changes: reflection and dynamic loading are limited.
cards/8/q: Turn on Native AOT in the project file
cards/8/explain: Set PublishAot=true, and dotnet publish builds a native file for the target platform.
cards/9/pairs/1/1: Precompiled code and CIL in one file
